questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a documentation template actually standardize?
options: The actual reasoning and decisions an architect makes for a specific solution
The exact Apex code every project must use
The structure — which sections exist, in what order, with what headings — while deliberately leaving the real content and judgment to the architect
The specific vendor-mandated wording of every sentence in the document
questions.explain: A template fixes structure (sections, order, expected tables) so architects don't reinvent the document skeleton each time, but it deliberately leaves the actual reasoning and trade-offs — the real design work — to the architect filling it in.

questions.q: What is the 'over-templating' failure mode this lesson describes?
options: A template with too few sections to be useful
An architect filling in every section because the template demands it, including sections that don't apply, producing a long, inconsistent document that buries what actually matters
A template that is reviewed too frequently
A template that has no version number
questions.explain: Over-templating happens when a rigid template forces box-ticking content for irrelevant sections, making the resulting document longer and harder to read rather than more useful.

questions.q: What fix does this lesson recommend for a template section that doesn't apply to a particular solution?
options: Silently omit the section entirely with no explanation
Pad the section with unrelated content so it looks complete
Explicitly state 'Not applicable — [one-sentence reason]' rather than silently omitting or padding the section
Delete the entire template and start over without one
questions.explain: The lesson's fix is to make a section's presence conditional on relevance, but when it doesn't apply, to say so explicitly with a one-sentence reason, rather than silently omitting it (which looks like an oversight) or padding it with irrelevant content.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a documentation template itself needs an owner and a version, not just the documents produced from it?
options: Because Salesforce requires all templates to be version-controlled by law
Because templates automatically expire after one year
Because only the CTA Review Board is allowed to maintain templates

Because a template that never gets revisited accumulates the same kind of rot as an individual document — a section that fit the original kind of project stops fitting as the team's work changes, and nobody updates it without a named owner
questions.explain: Without a named owner and version, a template drifts out of fit with the team's actual work the same way an individual document rots (Lesson 15) — the fix is the same discipline: ownership and periodic review, applied to the template itself.

questions.q: In the minimal SDD template skeleton this lesson provides, where does the access matrix from Lesson 14 belong?
options: Section 6, Security and Sharing Model
Section 2, System Context
Section 9, Assumptions and Open Items
The Appendix, Executive Summary
questions.explain: The template skeleton places the access matrix inside Section 6, Security and Sharing Model, consistent with Lesson 14's coverage of documenting the sharing model using that artifact.
